messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to use unmarked to run Hierarchical Distance Sampling models to estimate density of a songbird species using site covariates. Because I had repeated visits (each site was surveyed 3 times) I'm using gdistsamp, but I'm having a problem with my code. When I order my distances and then truncate them all my sites that were visited but where I didn't have any observations are removed. I've analyzed distance sampling data using the distance software before and I know this are important otherwise I can bias my estimate. Can someone help me with this?

Here is my code:

## Creates a data frame containing the distance data
dists<-data[,c(3,4,7)]

dists$sample.label <- as.factor(dists$sample.label)  #convert point transects label into a categorical variable
dists$replica <- as.factor(dists$replica)  #convert replica into a categorical variable

## Method used to include points which were surveyed but where no individuals were detected.
levels(dists$sample.label) <- c(levels(dists$sample.label), "sp049", "sp054", "sp074", "sp084", "sp085", "sp086")

## Histogram of the distances
hist(dists$distance)

dists.order <- dists[order(dists$distance), ] #this orders the data from small to large radial distances

# Creating an object to tell R where I want to truncate the data
distCut = 60

dists.trunc <-  dists.order[which(dists.order$distance < distCut), ]

## Binned data by 10 m intervals
cutpt <- seq(0, distCut, by=10)

yDat <- formatDistData(dists.trunc, distCol="distance", transectNameCol="sample.label", dist.breaks = cutpt, occasionCol="replica")  #create distance categories (m).
head(yDat)

# Read in and inspect the covariates that will be used to model effects on p and density.

covs <- read.csv("CovHDS.csv", sep=";")

# Create the unmarked dataframe.
umf <- unmarkedFrameGDS(y=as.matrix(yDat), numPrimary=3, survey="point", siteCovs=covs,dist.breaks=cutpt, unitsIn="m")

null.model<- gdistsamp(~1,~1,~1, umf, keyfun = "halfnorm", mixture = "NB", output = "density",unitsOut = "ha")

Thank you,

Fernanda Alves.

messages.body_plain:
What are the dimensions of your dists.trunc, yDat, and covs tables, and the umf? Sounds like your umf is getting the # rows/points from the yDat table, but I can't see why that would be from your code. Also, does dists.trunc have any rows with count = NA or zero? Perhaps post the structure and dimensions of each table and it will help us figure it out.

I don't believe there is any need to order the data from small to large radial distances so you can skip that step.

Also, I've found (rather I suspect) that gdistsamp has trouble distinguishing detection and availability in the three level hierarchical for the vast majority of birds for which I've calculated models. I believe this has to do with the field methods where we sample within a season during a time when there is typically minimal change in availability (eg. all visits within a single breeding season, etc.). So, unless you have reason to believe that there are major differences in availability across your three visits, such as overlapping migration periods or something like that, then I would recommend using distsamp.

After dusting off (and attempting to use) some code that Richard kindly helped me develop some time ago, I realize that I don't completely understand what I've been doing with the code.

The survey had two observers who collected data using a dependent double observer method on two occasions. So the y data consist of four columns of counts by the (1) primary observer on the first occasion; (2) secondary observer on the first occasion; (3) primary observer on the second occasion; (4) secondary observer on the second occasion.

  M <- nrow(p)

  return(pi)

obsToY <- matrix(1, 2, 2)

Here's a guess as to the underlying issue that you're having:

colext uses a parameterization of the dynamic occupancy model where occupancy is determined by 2T - 1 parameters (with T being the number of seasons).  Those parameters (would can be functions of other variables) are psi(1), extinction(1), ..., extinction(T-1), colonization(1),...,colonization(T-1).

Because of this parameterization, psi(2), psi(3),...,psi(T) are not modeled directly but only through the 2T - 1 parameters given above.  So if something that changes with season (but is essentially constant within a season - see Brittany Mosher's excellent comment), the only way to include such variables is with their inclusion as site covariates (constant across all seasons) and yearly-site covariates as they affect the colonization and extinction parameters.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

have you considered using what Andy calls "stacking the years" ? That is, treat the primary seasons as independent, stack their data all on top of each other and fit a static occupancy model using occu() with primary season as a factor (if you want to contrast all years) or as a continuous explanatory variable (if you want to estimate a trend).

As I see it, you commit a tiny bit of pseudoreplication (treating observations from same site across different primary occasions as independent), but that's probably not so bad.

Best regards  --- Marc

Here's a guess as to the underlying issue that you're having:

colext uses a parameterization of the dynamic occupancy model where occupancy is determined by 2T - 1 parameters (with T being the number of seasons).  Those parameters (would can be functions of other variables) are psi(1), extinction(1), ..., extinction(T-1), colonization(1),...,colonization(T-1).

Because of this parameterization, psi(2), psi(3),...,psi(T) are not modeled directly but only through the 2T - 1 parameters given above.  So if something that changes with season (but is essentially constant within a season - see Brittany Mosher's excellent comment), the only way to include such variables is with their inclusion as site covariates (constant across all seasons) and yearly-site covariates as they affect the colonization and extinction parameters.

But your desire to use mst, ssr, and msw to model psi(1), psi(2),..., psi(T) is certainly legitimate (assuming that is what you want).  But that can't be done directly (in my opinion but I would welcome being wrong about that) with the parameterization that colext uses.

But there is hope!  (Well, maybe.)  I've put together a draft manuscript (in internal review) that models psi(1), psi(2),...,psi(T) directly along with the dependence from year-to-year.  It, too, uses a parameterization of 2T - 1 parameters and produces models equivalent to colext,  Same underlying theory.  Just a different (but equivalent) parameterization.  I'm willing to share the draft to any that might be interested.

Jim

Two things:

-                      Your data set is very small

-                      Probably the NegBin model is not identifiable (see this paper Dennis, E.B., Morgan, B.J.T., Ridout, M.S. 2015. Computational aspects of N-mixture models. Biometrics 71, 237–246): estimability can be assessed by re-fitting the model for increasing values of the internal tuning “parameter” K (e.g., setting it to 500, 1000 etc). If the AIC and estimates keep changing, then the parameters are not identifiable. This happens often with the NegBin mixtures, but only rarely with the Poisson and ZIP mixtures.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: Question about point-specific abundance estimates and ranef()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I'm currently trying to estimate point-specific abundances for a set of 137 locations where we conducted 3 rounds of point-count surveys, with each round of surveys conducted by a different observer. Because of the multiple visits/observers I have fit all of my models using gdistsamp() and unmarkedFrameGDS(). I have completed the model selection process and settled on one model using a hazard rate key function and including observer as a covariate to detection, that is most strongly supported and fits the data well.

I now want to use this model to estimate the true abundance at each site corrected for imperfect detection. Based on some of my previous research online and through this discussion group, my impression is that to get point-specific abundance estimates from this model I need to use the ranef() function and have essentially done:

top.model <- gdistsamp(~1, ~1, ~observer, data = data, keyfun = "hazard")
re <- ranef(top.model)
re

For all of the sites where I detected birds the resulting estimated abundances seem reasonable and correlate roughly with the number of detected birds at each point, however I also get back a very specific abundance estimate (11.54) for every site where no birds were ever detected. What's more, this abundance estimate is quite a bit higher than many of the sites where I did detect birds (mean abundance at sites with birds detected = ~12, range = 5.6 to 18.8).

I have every reason to believe that sites with no detections truly had no birds (or potentially only very few), and so I feel like the predicted abundance at all of those sites should be 0.

Can anyone explain to me why I'm getting such high abundance estimates at sites with no detections and how to correct this? Am I mistaken about ranef returning point-specific abundance estimates or am I using it incorrectly, or alternatively is there a better method I should be using to estimate point specific abundances?

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Nathaniel Behl

M.S. student, Benkman Lab
Department of Zoology and Physiology
University of Wyoming

Those parameters (would can be functions of other variables) are psi(1), extinction(1), ..., extinction(T-1), colonization(1),...,colonization(T-1).
>
> Because of this parameterization, psi(2), psi(3),...,psi(T) are not modeled directly but only through the 2T - 1 parameters given above. >

messages.subject: Re: Question about point-specific abundance estimates and ranef()
messages.subject_clean: Question about point-specific abundance estimates and ranef()
messages.body_plain:
Nathaniel, I think you can expect to have >0 estimates at zero-count sites using ranef().  My understanding is that ranef() derives estimates from an empirical Bayes procedure, of which the actual count is only one component (see Royle 2004, Royle & Nichols 2003).  I get >0 estimates at zero count sites all the time with pcount and occupancy modeling.  Having said that, it seems like your estimates are definitely too high: I don't think a site with >0 count should have a lower abundance estimate than a site with a zero count?  Maybe it's possible, but I haven't seen it.  One thing that jumps out at me is that your only covariate is observer and you have no availability or abundance covariates.  Both detection and availability could be affected by time, date, and weather variables.  Abundance of course by habitat characteristics, site, etc.  Did you try any of those?

I also noticed a few posts earlier than yours that someone recommended using just distsamp instead of gdistsamp if possible.  Or you could use pcount if you feel okay assuming a closed population across your three surveys (or at least immigration equaling emigration).  Then you would not use the distance estimates.  Distance estimates in point counts can be not only way off but also strongly biased, so it's worth thinking about whether they're the problem.

Mike Worland

On Wednesday, February 22, 2017 at 2:15:05 PM UTC-6, Nathaniel Behl wrote:
> Hi all,
> I'm currently trying to estimate point-specific abundances for a set of 137 locations where we conducted 3 rounds of point-count surveys, with each round of surveys conducted by a different observer. Because of the multiple visits/observers I have fit all of my models using gdistsamp() and unmarkedFrameGDS(). I have completed the model selection process and settled on one model using a hazard rate key function and including observer as a covariate to detection, that is most strongly supported and fits the data well.
>
> I now want to use this model to estimate the true abundance at each site corrected for imperfect detection. Based on some of my previous research online and through this discussion group, my impression is that to get point-specific abundance estimates from this model I need to use the ranef() function and have essentially done:
>
> top.model <- gdistsamp(~1, ~1, ~observer, data = data, keyfun = "hazard")
> re <- ranef(top.model)
> re
>
> For all of the sites where I detected birds the resulting estimated abundances seem reasonable and correlate roughly with the number of detected birds at each point, however I also get back a very specific abundance estimate (11.54) for every site where no birds were ever detected. What's more, this abundance estimate is quite a bit higher than many of the sites where I did detect birds (mean abundance at sites with birds detected = ~12, range = 5.6 to 18.8).

> I have every reason to believe that sites with no detections truly had no birds (or potentially only very few), and so I feel like the predicted abundance at all of those sites should be 0.
>
> Can anyone explain to me why I'm getting such high abundance estimates at sites with no detections and how to correct this? Am I mistaken about ranef returning point-specific abundance estimates or am I using it incorrectly, or alternatively is there a better method I should be using to estimate point specific abundances?

Hi Nathaniel,

The ranef point estimate (the mean, at least) cannot be be zero, although the mode can. Derived density estimates (lambda* phi/area) might look more reasonable.  What do the estimates of p/phi look like? It seems likely that either detection or availability actually are quite low (i.e., sparse data), or that there is a lot of unexplained heterogeneity (i.e., highly variable counts across time/space) that might mess things up. I'm guessing that the issue is #2. Your model assumes that the number of birds available for detection at each site during each visit comes from the same mixture of distributions.  The probability of a site having 0 abundance given an expected value of 11 and Poisson variation is about 0.002%.

John

messages.body_plain:
I recommend using distsamp instead. Yes gdistsamp allows you to incorporate the repeated visits explicitly, but in practice I don't think it's achieving what you hoped. First, the gdistsamp formula is in the order 1) lambda (abundance) 2) phi (availability) and 3) p (detection) and you have put the observer covariate in the detection function, when according to your explanation I would think it should be a factor in availability?

In practice, unless there is a significant reason why you think availability would change between visits (e.g. temporary or annual migration) then gdistsamp I think has trouble attributing non-detections among the p and phi models. I would expect also that your lack of covariates on lambda has led to difficulty assigning variable abundance values among sites, try changing observer to the availability model and adding a few covariates to abundance.

If you don't think there are major shifts in availability between visits, and even if there is a large difference in skill level among your observers, then if every site got three visits and three observers then all have roughly identical effort assuming you used standardized field sampling protocols. Therefore gdistsamp is probably not necessary and I'm guessing will continue to give you unsatisfactory results.

On Wednesday, February 22, 2017 at 12:15:05 PM UTC-8, Nathaniel Behl wrote:
> Hi all,
> I'm currently trying to estimate point-specific abundances for a set of 137 locations where we conducted 3 rounds of point-count surveys, with each round of surveys conducted by a different observer. Because of the multiple visits/observers I have fit all of my models using gdistsamp() and unmarkedFrameGDS(). I have completed the model selection process and settled on one model using a hazard rate key function and including observer as a covariate to detection, that is most strongly supported and fits the data well.
>
> I now want to use this model to estimate the true abundance at each site corrected for imperfect detection. Based on some of my previous research online and through this discussion group, my impression is that to get point-specific abundance estimates from this model I need to use the ranef() function and have essentially done:
>
> top.model <- gdistsamp(~1, ~1, ~observer, data = data, keyfun = "hazard")
> re <- ranef(top.model)
> re
>
> For all of the sites where I detected birds the resulting estimated abundances seem reasonable and correlate roughly with the number of detected birds at each point, however I also get back a very specific abundance estimate (11.54) for every site where no birds were ever detected. What's more, this abundance estimate is quite a bit higher than many of the sites where I did detect birds (mean abundance at sites with birds detected = ~12, range = 5.6 to 18.8).
>
> I have every reason to believe that sites with no detections truly had no birds (or potentially only very few), and so I feel like the predicted abundance at all of those sites should be 0.
>
> Can anyone explain to me why I'm getting such high abundance estimates at sites with no detections and how to correct this? Am I mistaken about ranef returning point-specific abundance estimates or am I using it incorrectly, or alternatively is there a better method I should be using to estimate point specific abundances?

> Nathaniel Behl
